claims.text: Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 typically has residual porosity.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 can have insufficient mechanical strength for demanding plating environments.
Spark plasma sintering can densify ZrB2 at approximately 1800–2000 °C, below the temperature required for conventional sintering.
SPS applies rapid pulsed current and uniaxial pressure during ZrB2 consolidation.
SPS will produce enhanced densification and a finer-grained ZrB2 microstructure with reduced porosity.
Rapid heating and pressure-assisted diffusion during SPS lead to stronger grain boundaries and fewer defect sites.
Pulsed electric current and applied pressure accelerate diffusion and sintering kinetics in ZrB2.
Accelerated sintering kinetics promote rapid ZrB2 densification at lower temperatures.
Residual pores and grain-boundary voids act as initiation sites for holes and microcracks during liquid plating operations.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will achieve full densification at approximately 2000 °C.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will contain fewer residual pores than conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2.
Reduced porosity in SPS-processed ZrB2 will improve flexural strength, fracture toughness, and structural integrity.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will exhibit less hole formation and fewer component failures during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
The proposed mechanism applies when ZrB2 densification is dominated by solid-state diffusion and grain-boundary consolidation.
The proposed comparison assumes that SPS processing preserves an essentially single-phase ZrB2 composition.
Inadequate control of the SPS atmosphere or pressure may limit its effectiveness.
